- s. EU The 6th Anti-Money Laundering Directive (6MLD) standardizes UBO definitions across the European Union, which covers both ownership and control. The EU definition of a UBO includes an individual with more than 25% ownership or voting rights, or other ownership interests, whether directly or indirectly. Indirect ownership needs to be calculated through the full ownership chain. The 25% standard applies broadly; however, for certain high-risk sectors, Member States may impose lower UBO thresholds—down to a minimum of 15%—provided they receive approval from the European Commission. What constitutes “control” includes rights to appoint/remove board members, veto rights, and influence via agreements or family ties. A few things stand out in that definition: A UBO must be a natural person: a human being, not another company. You can't identify a holding company as a UBO. Wie kann ein wirtschaftlich Berechtigter (UBO) einer in Deutschland eingetragenen GmbH rechtskonform identifiziert und dokumentiert werden?

Gemäß den im Kontext bereitgestellten Informationen muss der wirtschaftlich Berechtigte (UBO) einer in Deutschland eingetragenen GmbH wie folgt identifiziert und dokumentiert werden:

1.  **Schwellenwert anwenden:** Eine natürliche Person ist UBO, wenn sie **mehr als 25%** der Anteile oder Stimmrechte hält (unter dem aktuellen EU-Rahmenwerk 4AMLD/5AMLD). Unter der kommenden AMLR (Verordnung EU 2024/1624) ändert sich dies auf **25% oder mehr** [from https://speedydd.com/articles/who-is-a-ubo-definition-and-requirements].
2.  **Natürliche Person identifizieren:** Ein UBO muss immer eine **natürliche Person** (ein Mensch) sein. Führt die Beteiligungskette zu einem Unternehmen, muss durch dieses Unternehmen hindurchgesehen werden, um die dahinterstehende Einzelperson zu finden [from https://speedydd.com/articles/who-is-a-ubo-definition-and-requirements].
3.  **Ersatzregelung bei Nichtidentifizierbarkeit:** Kann nach Anwendung der Eigentums- und Kontrolltests kein UBO gefunden werden, muss stattdessen der **leitende leitende Angestellte** (senior managing official) der GmbH identifiziert und verifiziert werden [from https://speedydd.com/articles/who-is-a-ubo-definition-and-requirements].

En français : quelle autorité contrôle les exportations de matériel de guerre en France, et que doit faire l'exportateur ?

L'autorité compétente est la CIEEMG (Commission Interministérielle pour l'Étude des Exportations de Matériels de Guerre), dont les travaux sont coordonnés par le SGDSN (Secrétariat général de la défense et de la sécurité nationale).

La licence est une AEMG (Autorisation d'Exportation de Matériels de Guerre), régie par le Code de la défense. Les biens à double usage relèvent d'un circuit distinct, le SBDU (Service des Biens à Double Usage), au titre du règlement (UE) 2021/821.

What is Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and how does it differ from Direct Commercial Sales for a supplier?

FMS (Foreign Military Sales) is a government-to-government channel administered by DSCA (Defense Security Cooperation Agency) in the US Department of Defense. The foreign government contracts with the US Government, and the US Government contracts the vendor. Major cases require Congressional notification, which DSCA publishes — those notices are public and are the earliest reliable signal of a pending sale.

DCS (Direct Commercial Sales) is the alternative: the vendor contracts the foreign customer directly, under an ITAR licence issued by DDTC.

What this means for a supplier: under FMS your customer is the US Government, not the end country — pricing, terms and contracting flow through DoD, and you cannot negotiate directly with the foreign buyer on the case. The practical action is to watch DSCA Congressional notifications for your platform and country, then position with the US programme office rather than the foreign ministry, because by the time the case is notified the requirement is already defined.

A defence tender you are tracking issues an amendment two weeks before the deadline. What should you actually do?

An amendment is a substantive event, not an administrative one. In the EU it is published as a corrigendum on TED (Tenders Electronic Daily) against the original contract notice, under Directive 2009/81/EC for defence and security procurement. It commonly does three things: changes technical requirements, changes eligibility or certification demands, and resets or extends the submission deadline.

What to do, in order: re-read the eligibility clauses first, because an amendment is the most common point at which a national-content, security-clearance or prior-experience requirement is introduced that silently disqualifies a bidder who was compliant under the original notice. Then re-check the deadline — an extension may also reopen the clarification window, which is your only lawful route to challenge a restrictive specification. Then re-run the bid/no-bid decision rather than assuming the earlier one holds.

The failure mode to avoid is treating an amendment as a date change and continuing a bid you have just become ineligible for.

What are industrial offsets in defence procurement and what do they oblige a winning supplier to do?

An offset is a compensation obligation imposed by the buying country as a condition of a defence contract — typically local production, technology transfer, local sourcing, training or investment, valued as a percentage of the contract and sometimes exceeding 100%.

What it obliges: the obligation is contractual and usually carries liquidated damages and a bank guarantee. It runs for years after delivery, is tracked by an offset authority in the buying ministry, and credit is granted only for activity that authority accepts — not for whatever the supplier happens to spend locally.

The action at bid stage is to price the offset as a cost line with its own risk reserve, confirm which activities earn credit and at what multiplier BEFORE committing, and check whether the technology transfer implied is itself export-licensable. A supplier who wins the contract and then discovers the transfer needs a licence the home state will refuse has bought a penalty, not a sale.

What is a UBO and why is the 25% threshold a trap in defence due diligence?

A UBO (ultimate beneficial owner) is the natural person who ultimately owns or controls an entity. Most registers and AML frameworks use an indicative threshold around 25% of shares or voting rights.

Why the threshold is a trap: 25% is a reporting trigger, not a definition of control. Control can sit below it through shareholder agreements, golden shares, board appointment rights, veto rights, nominee arrangements, or a chain of entities each holding under the threshold. A sanctioned person holding 24% in three layers appears nowhere and controls the company.

What to do: treat a clean 25% screen as the START of the enquiry. Trace the ownership chain to natural persons rather than stopping at the first corporate parent, ask for the shareholder agreement rather than only the register extract, and screen identified persons and their known associates. Where the chain cannot be resolved, record it as an unresolved control question — not as a clean result. An unverifiable owner is a finding.

An entity is not on the OFAC SDN list but is 60% owned by someone who is. Is it blocked?

Yes. Under OFAC's 50 Percent Rule, an entity owned 50% or more, directly or indirectly, by one or more blocked persons is itself blocked — even though it is not named on the SDN list. Ownership aggregates across multiple blocked persons.

Two consequences practitioners miss. First, the list is not the population: screening a name against the SDN list and getting no hit does not establish that the counterparty is permissible. Second, OFAC treats 50% as a bright line for blocking, but it also cautions about entities controlled by blocked persons below that level — those are not automatically blocked yet carry real risk.

What to do: resolve ownership percentages, aggregate blocked-person holdings, and block at 50% or more. Below 50% with evident control, escalate rather than clear, and record the reasoning. The EU and UK operate their own ownership-and-control tests that are similar in intent but not identical in wording, so a multi-jurisdiction transaction must be tested against each regime, not just the US one.

The recognised indicators are behavioural and commercial rather than technical: a customer whose business has no plausible use for the item; a freight-forwarder or trading intermediary as the named end user; a shipping route or transhipment point inconsistent with the stated destination; willingness to pay a premium with unusual payment terms; refusal of installation, training or after-sales support that the product normally requires; a newly incorporated counterparty with no trading history; and requests to under-declare value or mis-describe the goods.

Where the flag cannot be resolved, decline: the exporter carries the licence obligation regardless of what the customer asserted, and 'we were told it was civil' is not a defence.

A country announces a large increase in its defence budget. What does that actually tell a supplier, and what should they do?

Less than it appears. An announced headline figure is a political commitment, not contractible demand. Check whether the increase is new money or reprofiled from later years, whether it is capital or operating, and whether the country's absorption capacity — its procurement staffing and past execution rate — can actually spend it. How should an active conflict change a defence supplier's assessment of a market?

In two directions at once, and conflating them is the common error. Demand for consumables, munitions, sustainment and ISR typically rises quickly, while major new platform programmes often slow as funds are redirected to immediate needs.

Against that, risk rises sharply: export licences to a party to a conflict become harder or impossible; end-use assurance weakens because materiel moves; diversion and re-transfer risk increases; and reputational and legal exposure under the ATT risk criteria and international humanitarian law becomes live rather than theoretical.

What to do: separate the demand signal from the licensability question and answer the licensing one first, because it is binary. Check whether the destination is subject to an embargo or a policy of denial, whether neighbouring-state routes create a diversion path, and whether existing licences remain valid — states frequently suspend extant licences on conflict onset. A pipeline that cannot be licensed is not a pipeline.

Age changes what a fact can support, not merely how confident it is. Every result about a company traces back to one original source. How should that be handled?

As a single point of failure, and it must be stated. Wide repetition across many outlets is not corroboration when all of them derive from the same original — this is the most common way an unverified claim acquires the appearance of consensus. Press aggregation, database records that ingest the same filing, and machine-translated reprints all inflate apparent coverage without adding evidence.

What to do: identify the original source and assess it on its own merits — who published it, on what evidence, with what interest. Then attempt genuinely independent corroboration: a primary filing, a regulator, a court record, or a party with no relationship to the original.

If none exists, report the finding as single-sourced and name the source. The operator's action is to treat it as directional and weight it accordingly — not to discard it, and not to rely on it as established fact.

How do sanctions actually work in Latin America, and what should a supplier check before a transaction there?

The dominant regime is unilateral rather than multilateral. OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control, US Treasury) runs country programmes — Venezuela, Cuba and Nicaragua are the long-standing ones — plus the global list-based programmes such as SDNTK for narcotics trafficking. The EU maintains its own restrictive measures on some of the same countries, and they are NOT identical in scope. UN Security Council measures cover far less of the region than most people assume.

The practical consequence: a counterparty can be lawful for an EU exporter and blocked for a US-touching transaction, and the trigger is often not nationality but US nexus — a dollar-clearing payment, a US-origin component, or a US person in the chain.

How does NATO procurement actually work, and what determines whether a company can win work?

NATO buys in three distinct ways and they have different rules. NSPA (NATO Support and Procurement Agency) runs common-funded and nation-delegated acquisition and sustainment. The NCIA (NATO Communications and Information Agency) handles C4ISR and communications. And the overwhelming majority of NATO-relevant spend is NATIONAL — member states buying their own equipment to meet NATO capability targets.

What determines eligibility: for common-funded work, a company generally competes through its national delegation and must be registered and sponsored — being technically capable is not sufficient and not the gating factor. Framework agreements and basic ordering agreements are frequently the actual route to work, so presence on the framework beforehand decides who can bid at all.

What to do: register through the national NATO delegation or national NSPA point of contact first, pursue framework inclusion as an objective in its own right, and separate NATO-badged opportunities from national ones — they are advertised, competed and awarded under different rules, and conflating them wastes capture effort.

What rules govern European defence procurement, and where do suppliers actually lose?

Directive 2009/81/EC governs defence and security procurement in the EU, with notices published on TED (Tenders Electronic Daily). Article 346 TFEU allows a member state to exempt a contract where essential security interests are at stake — an exemption that is narrower than commonly assumed but is used, and when used removes the competition entirely. The European Defence Fund co-finances collaborative R&D under eligibility conditions concerning EU ownership and control of participants.

Where suppliers lose: not on technical score but on eligibility and process. Security clearance requirements for personnel and facilities that cannot be obtained within the timetable; national-content or industrial-participation conditions; security-of-supply undertakings that a non-domestic bidder cannot credibly give; and missed clarification windows, which are usually the only lawful moment to challenge a restrictive specification.

What to do: read the eligibility and security clauses before the technical requirement, decide bid/no-bid on those, and use the clarification window deliberately — after it closes, a restrictive spec is settled.

What characterises defence procurement in Spanish-speaking Latin America, and what should a supplier plan for?

What technical and sustainment factors decide defence equipment outcomes in Southern Africa?

Environment and sustainment dominate, more than headline performance. Equipment faces heat, dust and long logistics distances, and availability is limited by the spares and maintenance chain rather than by the platform's specification. Fleets are often mixed-origin and ageing, so obsolescence management and the ability to integrate with existing systems matter more than a capability increment.

South Africa is the region's significant defence-industrial base and a possible partner or competitor depending on the segment, which changes whether a local relationship is a route to market or a barrier.

What to do: lead the technical proposition with availability and through-life support — demonstrated MTBF (mean time between failures) in comparable conditions, ILS (integrated logistics support) provisioning, spares provisioning, and local maintenance capability — rather than peak performance. Check whether sustaining the existing fleet touches equipment of sanctioned origin, since the support contract can be restricted where the original sale was not, and confirm any technology transfer implied by local maintenance is licensable from the home state.

How should a supplier read the competitive landscape in North Africa?

The defining feature is supplier diversification as deliberate policy. States in the region have historically operated mixed inventories — Russian, Chinese, European and US origin in the same force — and treat multi-sourcing as strategic autonomy rather than an accident of history. Competition is therefore rarely a straight product comparison.

What actually decides outcomes: financing terms, offset and local-industrialisation commitments, technology transfer, political relationship, and the credibility of long-term support. A technically superior offer without financing frequently loses to an inferior one with it.

What to do: map the incumbent by SEGMENT rather than by country — an incumbent in armour tells you little about air defence — and identify what the customer cannot obtain from its existing suppliers, because that gap is the entry point. Then test early whether the transfer and support the customer will demand is licensable from your home state, since a US or European supplier faces constraints a competitor may not, and that constraint is a competitive fact, not a footnote.
